source_text: Qua ergo tu impudentia et approbas sententiam meam, et tuum dogma non deseris; cum sententiae utriusque partis ita nullo possint foedere copulari, ut enuntiatorum opposita pariter non participant veritati? Quomodo ergo ego si consentirem naturale esse peccatum, necesse erat ut deciderem de iure sententiae, quae praescribit, nisi in voluntate libera peccatum esse non posse; ita tu e regione consentiens me bene dixisse, qui pronuntiavi nullum esse sine voluntate peccatum, reicere statim debuisti illam opinionem, qua peccatum naturale credebas.
pass_a_gloss: By what shamelessness therefore do you both approve my sentence and not desert your dogma; when the sentences of each part can by no treaty be coupled, so that the opposites of the utterances equally do not share in truth? How therefore if I consented that sin is natural, it was necessary that I fall from the right of the sentence which prescribes that sin cannot be except in a free will; so you from the opposite side, consenting that I spoke well, I who pronounced that there is no sin without will, ought immediately to have thrown off that opinion by which you believed a natural sin.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: With what shamelessness, then, do you both approve my statement and refuse to abandon your doctrine? The statements of the two sides cannot be joined by any agreement, since opposite assertions do not share the truth at the same time. If I agreed that sin was natural, I would necessarily fall away from the force of the statement that sin can exist only in free will. In the same way, you, by agreeing that I spoke rightly in declaring that no sin exists without will, should immediately have rejected the opinion by which you believed sin to be natural.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
